analysis.one_liner: Bars the Treasury from requiring banks to report account balances and deposit flows to the IRS.
analysis.headline: Backed by 49 of 50 Senate Republicans as cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would permanently prohibit the Treasury Department from requiring banks or other financial institutions to report account balances, transactions, or the money flowing into and out of customer accounts, while leaving in place any reporting already required by law at the time of enactment. It was written to block a Biden administration proposal under which banks would send the IRS aggregate account-flow data, a tool aimed at finding taxpayers who report less income than they actually take in. The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee on October 21, 2021 and received no hearing, no vote, and no further action before the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.who_benefits: Three groups gain. Banks and other financial institutions avoid the cost of tracking and transmitting gross flow data on every customer account. Taxpayers whose income is not automatically reported to the IRS — business owners, investors, and high earners who handle cash — avoid a new tool designed to reveal mismatches between what they report and what flows through their accounts. And account holders opposed to the government collecting their transaction data keep their information at their bank.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Banks and high earners with unreported income

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the Treasury Department from requiring any financial institution to report the inflows, outflows, balances, transactions, or transfers of any account it maintains.
Leaves existing reporting requirements untouched, so the current tax-reporting system continues as before.
Its stated purpose, reflected in its title, is preventing new government collection of bank account deposits and withdrawals.

analysis.who_pays: The cost falls on tax enforcement and on compliant taxpayers. Without flow data, the IRS must keep relying on self-reported income for money that is not automatically reported to it — the portion of income where underreporting is most common — and unpaid taxes shift onto wage earners whose taxes are withheld automatically, as well as onto public finances.

drawbacks.text: The ban applies to any new reporting requirement, with no income threshold, no limit on account size, and no carve-out for data that would target enforcement only at large or suspicious accounts — the only exception is for programs already in law on the date of enactment.

By blocking the collection of flow data, the bill keeps the IRS dependent on self-reporting for income that is not withheld from a paycheck, where underreporting is most common and hardest to detect; the resulting tax gap is borne by honest wage earners and public budgets.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers account holders real protection against the government receiving a comprehensive file on their financial lives — under the proposal it was written to stop, banks would have reported gross flows on accounts held by ordinary households as well as the wealthy. But that privacy protection is inseparable from the bill's other effect: it removes the easiest way for the IRS to see when someone reports far less income than moves through their accounts, and the cost of that blind spot lands on taxpayers who cannot underreport because their taxes are withheld. An honest supporter would acknowledge the bill protects the privacy of everyone, including precisely the people the enforcement proposal was designed to find.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced, nothing further ever happened to it, and the Congress ended without a vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Tim Scott introduced the bill on October 21, 2021, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
Forty-nine of the Senate's 50 Republicans signed on as cosponsors; no Democrat did.
The action history shows no hearing, markup, or floor action after the initial referral, and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

The bill would have prohibited Treasury from requiring institutions to report account inflows, outflows, balances, transactions, or transfers, except where such reporting was already required by law at enactment.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one changed position. The bill died without a vote, and the underlying Treasury reporting proposal was never enacted either, so the status quo held: banks face no new reporting duties, and the IRS received no new account data. Banks and taxpayers whose income is hard for the IRS to see are no worse off — and no better off — than before.

sides.party_line_note: All 49 cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat sponsored or cosponsored the bill, and no vote was ever taken.

industries.note: The bill spares banks the cost of computing and transmitting gross flow data on every customer account — a compliance burden the industry lobbied hard against. That saving comes at the expense of an enforcement tool aimed at collecting taxes the public is already owed, a cost that otherwise falls back on compliant taxpayers.

industries.industry: High-income taxpayers with non-withheld income (business owners, investors, cash-heavy businesses)
industries.note: The reporting proposal was built to compare income people report with the money actually moving through their accounts, the main blind spot in tax enforcement for people whose income is not withheld from a paycheck. The bill keeps that blind spot closed, so unpaid taxes continue to shift onto wage earners and public budgets.
